# Education in Finland
Education in Finland has deep historical roots tied to Lutheranism, emphasizing literacy for reading religious texts. The first Finnish university was established in 1640, and by the late 19th century, literacy reached over 80%. The early education system evolved from Swedish-language instruction to Finnish, becoming mandatory for all children by 1921. The current comprehensive education system mandates nine years of basic schooling (grades 1–9), with recent legislation extending compulsory education to include upper secondary school or vocational training until age 18. Schools are municipally funded and managed, with minimal private schooling limited to non-selective, tuition-free institutions, often faith-based or Steiner schools. Class sizes are small, with a strong emphasis on multilingualism, broad-based learning, outdoor activities, and minimal homework.
Finnish early childhood education, free and virtually universal, focuses on play-based learning and social development up to age seven. Upper secondary education divides into academic and vocational tracks, both free and offering national matriculation examinations crucial for university admission. Teachers hold master’s degrees, enjoy professional respect, and face competitive entry to training programs. Finnish tertiary education comprises universities focusing on research and universities of applied sciences, with merit-based, transparent admissions emphasizing comprehensive examinations over subjective criteria. Since 2017, tuition fees apply only to non-EEA students, aiming to enhance educational quality and international competitiveness. Finland actively promotes adult education and lifelong learning through diverse municipal and independent programs. Ongoing reforms include national curriculum changes emphasizing phenomenon-based learning and international educational export initiatives supporting Finnish pedagogy worldwide.
